intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene.

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that the KNO2 syndrome in the studied family is dominant and caused by a deleterious variant in the PAK2 gene.
checks.explanation: Monoallelic (heterozygous) PAK2 variant causes KNO2.

paragraphs.text: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is a disorder characterized by high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration with retinal detachment, and occipital encephalocele or scalp defect. Affected individuals have also shown intellectual disability, autistic behavior, and pulmonary abnormalities (Wilson et al., 1998; Antonarakis et al., 2021). Unlike the autosomal recessive form of Knobloch syndrome caused by COL18A1 mutation, KNO2 is not linked to COL18A1 (Menzel et al., 2004) and is caused by a dominant monoallelic variant in PAK2 (Antonarakis et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Wilson et al. (1998) reported 2 sibs from New Zealand with high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, and occipital encephalocele or a scalp lesion. In one sib the eye disease was severe and began very early. In the other sib the scalp defect was very mild. Both sibs appeared to have an unusual pulmonary lymphatic condition, and Wilson et al. (1998) suggested that mesoderm might be involved in the morphogenesis of the disorder.

checks.evidence_quote: We report on two sibs with high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration (VRD), and occipital encephalocoele or scalp lesion.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports the clinical findings but doesn't say the sibs were from New Zealand. That detail comes only from a later citing paper (Haghighi et al., 2014), not from this paper's own text.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) restudied the family reported by Wilson et al. (1998) and described the phenotype as Knobloch syndrome type 2 with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, and encephalocele. The 2 sibs had varying combinations of severe developmental delay, incomprehensible speech, and autism spectrum disorder.

checks.claim: Antonarakis et al. (2021) restudied the family with 2 affected sibs reported by Wilson et al. (1998).
checks.evidence_quote: We studied an historical pedigree (published in 1998) designated as KNO2
checks.explanation: The abstract mentions a pedigree published in 1998 with two affected siblings, but it does not name Wilson et al. as the original report.

checks.claim: Antonarakis et al. (2021) described the phenotype in the family of Wilson et al. (1998) as Knobloch syndrome type 2 with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, and encephalocele.
checks.evidence_quote: designated as KNO2 (Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, encephalocele)
checks.explanation: The abstract gives this phenotype description for the 1998 pedigree.

checks.claim: The 2 sibs in the family restudied by Antonarakis et al. (2021) had varying combinations of severe developmental delay, incomprehensible speech, and autism spectrum disorder.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not mention severe developmental delay, incomprehensible speech or ASD. Only a later citing paper (Yahia et al., 2024) describes these features. Any such detail would be in the full text, which was not supplied.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) found that KNO2 in the family they studied followed a dominant pattern. The heterozygous PAK2 mutation was apparently de novo in both affected sibs, which suggested germline mosaicism in one of the parents.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) excluded linkage to the COL18A1 locus on chromosome 21q22.3 in a New Zealand family with Knobloch syndrome. This provided evidence for a second Knobloch syndrome locus, which they called KNO2. Mutation analysis also excluded COL15A1 as the gene responsible for KNO2.

checks.claim: Menzel et al. (2004) excluded linkage to the COL18A1 locus on chromosome 21q22.3 in a New Zealand family with Knobloch syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic mutations in the COL18A1 gene on 21q22.3 were recently identified in KNO families. Analysis of two unrelated KNO families from Hungary and New Zealand
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the 21q22.3 location and reports that linkage to COL18A1 was excluded in the New Zealand family.

checks.claim: Exclusion of COL18A1 linkage in the New Zealand family provided evidence for a second Knobloch syndrome locus, called KNO2 by Menzel et al. (2004).
checks.evidence_quote: Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family, providing evidence for the existence of a second KNO locus. We named the second unmapped locus for Knobloch syndrome KNO2.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.explanation: The abstract gives this chromosomal location.

checks.claim: Menzel et al. (2004) excluded COL15A1 by mutation analysis as the gene responsible for KNO2.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis excluded COL15A1, a member of the multiplexin collagen subfamily similar to COL18A1, as being responsible for KNO2.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) confirmed that COL18A1 is involved in Knobloch syndrome by finding COL18A1 mutations in a Hungarian family. They showed genetic heterogeneity by excluding linkage to COL18A1 in a New Zealand family.

checks.claim: Menzel et al. (2004) found COL18A1 mutations in a Hungarian family with Knobloch syndrome, confirming COL18A1 involvement in Knobloch syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Analysis of two unrelated KNO families from Hungary and New Zealand allowed us to confirm the involvement of COL18A1 in the pathogenesis of KNO and to demonstrate the existence of genetic heterogeneity. Two COL18A1 mutations were identified in the Hungarian family
checks.explanation: The abstract reports COL18A1 mutations in the Hungarian family and says this confirmed COL18A1's role in KNO.

checks.claim: Menzel et al. (2004) showed genetic heterogeneity of Knobloch syndrome by excluding linkage to COL18A1 in a New Zealand family.
checks.evidence_quote: Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family, providing evidence for the existence of a second KNO locus.
checks.explanation: The abstract says the analysis showed genetic heterogeneity and that COL18A1 linkage was excluded in the New Zealand family.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) performed whole-exome sequencing on the 2 affected sibs originally reported by Wilson et al. (1998) and on their unaffected parents. They found a heterozygous glu435-to-lys (E435K) substitution in the PAK2 gene in both sibs. The variant appeared to be de novo in both sibs, suggesting germline mosaicism in one parent, but deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not detect mosaicism. The variant lies in the kinase domain of PAK2, and structural analysis predicted that it could compromise kinase activity. In transfected HEK293T cells, the E435K variant caused partial loss of kinase activity. Antonarakis et al. (2021) concluded that KNO2 in this family was dominant and caused by the PAK2 variant.

checks.claim: Antonarakis et al. (2021) performed whole-exome sequencing on the 2 affected sibs originally reported by Wilson et al. (1998) and on their unaffected parents.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole exome sequencing of the two affected siblings and the normal parents resulted in the identification of a PAK2 non-synonymous substitution p.(Glu435Lys) as a causative variant.
checks.explanation: WES was done on both affected sibs and their unaffected parents. The family is the 1998 pedigree, although Wilson is not named.

checks.evidence_quote: The variant was monoallelic and apparently de novo in both siblings
checks.explanation: Monoallelic means heterozygous. The variant is p.(Glu435Lys) in PAK2.

checks.evidence_quote: The variant was monoallelic and apparently de novo in both siblings indicating a likely germ-line mosaicism in one of the parents
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Structural analysis of the PAK2 p.(Glu435Lys) variant that is located in the kinase domain of the protein
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Structural analysis of the PAK2 p.(Glu435Lys) variant that is located in the kinase domain of the protein predicts a possible compromise in the kinase activity.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Functional analysis of the p.(Glu435Lys) PAK2 variant in transfected HEK293T cells results in a partial loss of the kinase activity.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2), originally reported by Wilson et al. (1998), Antonarakis et al. (2021) found a heterozygous glu435-to-lys (E435K) substitution in the kinase domain of the PAK2 gene by whole-exome sequencing. The mutation was apparently de novo in both sibs, suggesting parental germline mosaicism, but deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not detect mosaicism. In transfected HEK293T cells, the mutation caused partial loss of kinase activity.
